previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. Thompson was admitted for acute decompensated heart failure with worsening dyspnea, orthopnea, and lower extremity edema, with a 7 kg weight gain since his last discharge. He developed transient hypotension likely due to accidental doubling of his home medications, which resolved without intervention. He was treated with intravenous Lasix, later transitioned to oral Lasix 160 mg daily, achieving a discharge weight of 79.9 kg with improved symptoms. His INR dropped to 1.7, prompting bridging with heparin and warfarin dose adjustment to 3 mg daily. Metoprolol was restarted at 12.5 mg daily once blood pressure stabilized. Glyburide was held inpatient with transition to sliding scale insulin; atorvastatin and vitamin D were initiated. He was discharged home with home health services and follow-up in the heart failure clinic, with instructions to monitor weight and maintain anticoagulation.

Brief Hospital Course:
Mr. ___ is a ___ gentleman with a history of DM2, 
diastolic CHF s/p ICD, HTN, HTN, AVR on coumadin, cirrhosis, 
COPD, MI s/p RCA stents ___ who presented with severe LLE 
cellulitis.  He was treated with one week of IV Vancomycin/Zosyn 
and was discharged home to complete his course with one week of 
oral Bactrim/Augmentin.

ACTIVE ISSUES

# LEFT LOWER EXTREMITY CELLULITIS: now resolving.
Though he had no fever or leukocytosis, the clinical appearance 
of his LLE was concerning for cellulitis so he was started on IV 
antibiotics.  Initially Vancomycin but due to his diabetes, 
added Zosyn for gram negative/anaerobe coverage.  Team attempted 
to change to PO antibiotics after a couple of days but swelling 
and redness did not improve so he was again put on IV 
antibiotics.  He completed a 1 week course of Vanc/Zosyn and by 
then his exam was much improved.  Blood cultures were negative.  
Anticipate that he will need a longer course for his infection, 
so he is being discharged on one week of Bactrim/Augmentin.
Total course: Vancomycin (___), Zosyn (___). 
Plan for Bactrim/Augmentin from ___.  He will then follow 
up with his PCP ___ at ___ on ___.

INACTIVE ISSUES

# DIASTOLIC HEART FAILURE: stable.
No rales on exam, and lower leg swelling was attributed to his 
cellulitis.  He was continued on Torsemide and Metoprolol.
  
# TYPE TWO DIABETES: stable.
He was continued on his oral meds, except that his Metformin was 
held for 72H after his CT.  No major issues with hyperglycemia 
this admission.
  
# HYPERLIPIDEMIA: stable.
He was continued on Atorvastatin every other day.  
  
# HYPERTENSION: SBPs 90-100s.
He was continued on Metoprolol succinate.  
  
# H/O AVR: INR is 2.5 on discharge, within goal 2.0-2.5 (per 
PCP, goal 1.5-2.5).  
His dose was changed to 3mg daily for the past two days while 
hospitalized.  INR never dropped below 1.7.  He will follow up 
per usual routine at ___ clinic.
  
# CHRONIC HIP PAIN: stable.
He will continue on Oxycodone.  
  
# COPD: stable.  
No dyspnea, hypoxia, or oxygen requirement.  He was continued on 
his inhalers.
  
# LOOSE STOOL: resolved.
Soft stool, not watery.  Was likely due to excessive bowel 
regimen, no pain associated, no complaints at the time of 
discharge.  
    
# H/O UGIB:stable.
He was continued on protonix and sucralfate.  
  
# ANEMIA: Hct stable at ~30.
At baseline, has a history of chronic blood loss due to 
coumadin. Recent iron studies from ___ suggest iron deficiency 
(Ferritin<10) and very low hapto (?AVR and shearing).  He was 
continued on ferrous sulfate .

TRANSITIONAL ISSUES

# At upcoming PCP appointment, should have clinical exam of LLE 
to ensure that the cellulitis was adequately treated.

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  ___ with left lower extremity swelling and pain.

TECHNIQUE:  Doppler ultrasound.

FINDINGS:  There is normal compressibility, flow, and augmentation of the left
common femoral, superficial femoral, popliteal, and calf veins.

IMPRESSION:  No DVT.

RADIOGRAPHS OF THE LEFT TIBIA, FIBULA, AND ANKLE

HISTORY:  Left lower extremity swelling and cellulitis.  Question air.

COMPARISONS:  None.

TECHNIQUE:  Left tibia, fibula, and ankle, five views altogether.

FINDINGS:  There is no evidence for fracture, dislocation, or bone
destruction.  Vascular calcifications are present.  There is no evidence for
gas within the soft tissues.  Soft tissues appear swollen about the ankle. 
Slight degenerative changes involve the knee and ankle.  Mild degenerative
irregularities involve the mid foot.  A moderate subcalcaneal bone spur is
noted.

IMPRESSION:  No evidence for bone destruction or gas within soft tissues. 
Vascular calcifications.  Mild degenerative changes.

HISTORY:  ___ male with cellulitis of the left lower extremity, not
improving on IV antibiotics.  Assess for focal abscess or CT evidence of
osteomyelitis.

COMPARISON:  Lower extremity radiographs from ___

TECHNIQUE:  ___ MDCT axial images of the lower extremity were acquired with
intravenous contrast.  Images were displayed with 2.5-mm slice thickness. 
Bone and soft tissue algorithms were reviewed.  Coronal and sagittal
reformations were prepared.

CT OF THE LEFT LOWER EXTREMITY WITH INTRAVENOUS CONTRAST:  There is extensive
subcutaneous soft tissue edema surrounding the distal left lower extremity to
the level of the ankle and proximal left foot.  There is circumferential edema
and severe skin thickening which is nonspecific in appearance, though
corresponds with the history of cellulitis.  No rim-enhancing fluid collection
is identified within the surrounding soft tissues to suggest abscess
formation.  There is no soft tissue air.  Cortical margins are intact without
osteolysis to suggest osteomyelitis.  

There is no acute fracture or dislocation.  No bone destructive lesion is
identified.  

The popliteal artery, and distal branch vessels inclusive of the anterior
tibial, posterior tibial, and peroneal branches demonstrate dense
atherosclerotic calcifications.  Small dystrophic alcifications are seen
within the skin and anterior soft tissues of the left lower extremity.

IMPRESSION:

1.  Moderate-to-severe circumferential skin and subcutaneous edema surrounding
the distal left lower extremity and ankle, findings  consistent with
cellulitis per clinical history.

2.  No rim-enhancing fluid collection to suggest abscess formation.

3.  No CT evidence of osteomyelitis.  If there is ongoing clinical concern,
MRI would be a more sensitive modality for evaluation.
